TF Cold-Test Discharges as a Validation of the FDU, Coil and Supply Models

§1 — What the cold tests can validate, and what does not transfer

Two ITER TF coils have now been energised and fast-discharged in the Magnet Cold Test Facility (MCTB, building 55): TF07 on 22–28 May 2026, up to 10 kA, and TF17 on 24–28 September 2026, at 5–30 kA. Every discharge is archived at 80 kHz on the SDN archive. That covers the coil current at three points, the bypass, breaker and counter-pulse branch currents, the resistor current and voltage, the breaker and DC-line voltages, and the earthing voltage. A per-discharge record carries the controller's own event times. This is the only measured fast discharge of an ITER coil through an FDU of the ITER topology, and the plan uses it to test four parts of our model:

  • the commutation: bypass opening, the counter-pulse that drives the vacuum breaker to current zero, and the snubber and resistor transient that follow it;
  • the coil's passive response: the fast current drop as eddy and coupling currents take flux in the case, radial plates and conductor;
  • the discharge resistor's heating, and the resistance law it implies;
  • the test converter, whose TF07 flat top carried several times the ripple of TF17's;
  • the quench-detection signals, on the co-wound tapes and the pancake pairs, which TF07's converter noise degraded.

From those validated models, §11 then designs the current controllers for the remaining tests, the next TF coil and PF1, with stated phase and gain margins.

The topology transfers; the values do not. The test FDU is a main current-commutation unit and a backup, in series. The main unit is a bypass switch (BPS) beside a vacuum breaker (VCB), commutated by an oscillating counter-pulse circuit (CPC: L, C and a thyristor). The backup is a pyrobreaker (PB). The main CCU has four parallel branches: the BPS, two VCBs in series (each with an arc-voltage sensor), the oscillating zero-crossing circuit (the CPC), and an RC snubber. The main and backup CCUs in series sit in parallel with the resistor (FDR, 5 mΩ), so the snubber sees the resistor through the pyrobreaker, not directly. An earthing unit (EFD) holds the circuit's midpoint to ground. Sources: BFGEYD v1.2 PDF 4, 7, and the TF17 FDU commutation description the lead supplied on 20 October 2026, §7.1 with Figures 16 and 17 (its IDM uid is to be added). That is the ITER FDU topology which coil-circuit-playback-figures §8 models. The values are the test facility's own. Its resistor is about 5.5 mΩ, so τ is about 60 s. The ITER TF units are 0.111 Ω each, with τeq at 11 s. Cold-test currents are capped at 34 kA, half the ITER rating, and the voltage to ground at ±92 V (GFTG3P v1.0 slide 3), which is why the discharges are slow. So this plan validates methods, and the coil's own passive response, and reports the uncertainty each one carries into the ITER model. It never moves an ITER circuit parameter to the test facility's value. The rule is the same as in the memory note on the partner repository: mctb's resistor law and passive mode transfer as methods, while its test FDU's resistance and time constant do not.

They are cited by FR3D23 v1.0 PDF 3 and E9JSG8 v1.0 PDF 6. The CPC capacitance, inductance and charge voltage, the snubber values and the resistor module arrangement are therefore not held. §3 identifies the CPC from the data, and the other values stay stated assumptions until the documents are opened.

One finding already follows from these documents. mctb's discharge fit needed a constant 0.90 V drop in TF07's path and none in TF17's, and found that the two tests used different FFS legs (LA4 on TF07, LA5 on TF17) without a cause. FR3D23 supplies it: on TF07 the MFFS was held open, so the decaying current freewheeled through the TFFS thyristors, whose forward drop is that 0.9 V. On TF17 it took the mechanical contact. A thyristor leg on the freewheeling path is therefore worth a constant drop of about 0.9 V, and at the ITER TF voltages that is negligible.

No filter was added before TF17. The lead reported on 20 October 2026 that the mitigation was to run TF17 on one converter unit instead of two in parallel. Lucy's IDM index ends around 13 August 2026, so no indexed record confirms it, but the 80 kHz archive does. The table gives line amplitudes in volts over 10 s of flat top before each discharge, on the converter output PC:DV3:

25 Hz50 Hz100 Hz300 Hz600 Hz
TF07 10 kA1.982.381.852.081.76
TF17 10 kA0.010.150.666.302.74
TF17 30 kA0.030.442.074.940.32

Three readings follow. On TF17, 300 Hz dominates at about three times TF07's level. A 12-pulse pair cancels that line, so this is one 6-pulse unit running alone. The 25 Hz loop line fell from about 2–3 V to 0.01–0.03 V, consistent with one current loop in place of two independent bridge loops. And the ratio of the DC-line voltage DCL:DV9 to the converter voltage is the same on both coils (about 1.1 at 300 Hz, 1.6 at 600 Hz), so nothing was inserted between converter and DC line. TF17 thus traded the TF07 loop hunting for an uncancelled 300 Hz line. That trade shapes §11: with a bridge-balancing loop, both units can run again, and the 300 Hz cancellation returns.

What is measured, and how fast

A read on 20 October 2026 of the TF17 30 kA discharge (2026-09-28 12:54:48.301 UTC) shows that the 80 kHz sampling, 12.5 µs per sample, resolves the commutation:

  • the CPC fires 209.954 ms after the trigger;
  • the main-CCU current MCCU:LA6 rises from the 30 kA coil current to 43.6 kA at 211.22 ms, a quarter ring of about 1.27 ms;
  • the VCB reaches current zero at 211.916 ms;
  • the current is in the resistor at 213.495 ms;
  • the resistor voltage swings to −1.04 kV and its current reverses to −5.96 kA while the snubber and the CPC share the transfer.

The lead's commutation description (§1) fixes the channel map. PC:LA3 is the main current, equal to MCCU:LA6 in normal running with FDR:LA9 near zero. MCCU:LA6 is the main-CCU current, and MCCU:LA7 the VCB-branch current (the ammeter in Figure 17), which carried the 30 kA until the breaker's zero. BCCU:LA8 is the pyrobreaker current; MCCU:DV4 and BCCU:DV5 are the CCU voltages. Once the BPS has opened, the counter-pulse current is LA6 − LA7, and the 43.6 kA peak on LA6 is the whole main-CCU current while the resistor current goes negative. It is not the ring itself. Before this map was known, the two readings of the ring below were open. If 43.6 kA is the ring amplitude, a 3 kV charge and a 1.27 ms quarter ring give about 11 mF and 56 µH. If the ring rides on the 30 kA coil current, so that its amplitude is the 13.6 kA increment, the same reading gives about 3.7 mF and 178 µH. The two readings differ by a factor of three in C. §3's zero-current fit, where no coil current is present, settles it. Fronts shorter than about 25 µs, such as the snubber's own edge and the breaker arc, are below the sampling and are not resolved. The plan makes no claim about them from these data. The per-discharge records (MAG-MCTB-FD:*) carry the controller's estimates of each event time, plus the peak and minimum resistor, coil and ground voltages. On this discharge the resistor peak of 1.786 kV comes at 1.523 s, a second event well after the transfer, which §3 must attribute. MCCU:DV10 read zero throughout, and EFD:DV7 read within ±0.1 of zero, so §2 must establish their scaling, or that they are dead, before anything uses them.

The access recipe, read traps and server policy are those of mctb's UDA access record, implemented in iter_uda (~/Code/iter-uda), which this repository already uses in scripts/iter/uda/. The analysis mctb has already done is the comparison every section here must meet or explain: mctb's discharge fit, with ten discharges at 0.04–0.27 % rms, k² = 0.80 and τ2 = 0.49 s, and kF = 1.83 µΩ/MJ. The passive constants are already imported into the ITER model as winding_losses.CONDUCTOR_COUPLING_K2 and CONDUCTOR_COUPLING_TAU2_S. scripts/iter/tf_fast_discharge.py reproduces one cold test, but only from mctb's fitted constants.

§2 — The discharge store and its loader

Fetch every cold-test discharge once and hold it locally, so that no later section reads the archive. The fetch runs under MINT, as the scripts in scripts/iter/uda/ do: module purge; ml MINT/1.5.2-intel-2025b, with PYTHONPATH=~/Code/iter-uda/src and MINT's Python, not the project environment. It reads through iter_uda.uda.connect, which refuses the operators' server. The fleet node reaches both archives. For each discharge it saves:

  • raw 80 kHz data (decSamples=-1, spacing checked in the returned stamps) on every MAG-MCTB-PS-*_D channel, from 0.5 s before the trigger to 2 s after it, and from 1.3 s to 1.8 s after it, to cover the late resistor peak;
  • the envelope (avg, min, max) at about 12.5 ms over 480 s, on the same channels and on EQDD1/2:FC_V_D;
  • every field of every MAG-MCTB-FD:* record within ±10 s of the trigger, joined on t0, never on the pulse string;
  • the six FDU temperature sensors MAG-MCTB-PS-FDU:MTY4001–4006-TT-XI from the slow archive, from 1 h before to 6 h after;
  • for §8, 4 s of raw data on PC:DV3, PC:LA3, DCL:DV6, DCL:DV9, DCL:LA10, DCL:LA11 and EQDD1/2:FC_V_D at each flat top and on each ramp, at matched currents on both coils. Also any slow-archive per-bridge current channel, if the bridge currents CV1/CV2 (LA1, LA2) are archived anywhere. Search for them by pattern and record an empty result as a measurement.
  • for §10, every MAG-MCTB-EQDD1:* and MAG-MCTB-EQDD2:* channel, raw at 1 kHz, over each whole test: the ramp, the hold and 480 s of the discharge. That covers the co-wound tape (DPn_CW_V), DPn_RT_V and DPn_RP_V signals, the pancake-pair signals (DP17, DP26, DP35, DP42), FC_V, the busbar, lead, HX and terminal signals, QD_FDRQ and the QUENCH1/2 flags. Over the same windows, take the 80 kHz converter voltage and current at the same instants, so that §10 can form transfers. A channel that returns an empty interval (as DP4_RP_V did on TF17's 30 kA discharge) is recorded empty, beside a same-session read that returned data.

The discharges are TF17-1_FD/1–6 and TF17-1_ZC_FD/1–4; TF07_FD/1–11, of which those with current are located from the resistor current, as mctb does, if no record exists; and the August TF17 shots (TF17_FD/1, TF17_FD_B55/2, TF17_ZC_FD/1–5), catalogued whatever they turn out to be. This section is the single writer and owner of the store, with one layout: /home/ITER/mcintos/Code/power_convertor/data/mctb/<coil>/<window>.npz. Values are in SI units, keyed by archived channel name, with one time array per channel. Each window carries one JSON sidecar schema: coil, discharge, current, event time, sample rate per channel, front-end filter where known, query strings, server, read time, and the same-session positive-control read. The window kinds are each discharge (its raw commutation windows and its 480 s envelope), each flat top, each ramp, and each FDU opening from −50 ms to +200 ms. Those last three are also the windows quench-detection-converter-pickup asked for: flat tops at three matched currents of at least 10 s, one 10 A/s ramp, and every FDU opening. No later section writes to the store or reads the archive. The capture reuses what the repository already has. Flat tops and ramps are located with iter_uda.windows.activity_windows. Each reply is saved through the npz-and-receipt helper save_reply in the shared module scripts/iter/uda/capture.py. That module was consolidated when the store landed (merge 5ef491e5), and save_pf_window.py, dummy_load_sessions.py and dummy_load_windows.py all import it. Later fetches into the store use it too. The loader src/power_convertor/cold_test_data.py returns a discharge with its channels zero-corrected and sign-normalised. It takes zeros from the quiet tail, not from before the trigger, because before the trigger the resistor terminals carry the closed bypass path's voltage. It aligns the channels on the trigger and exposes the record times. Channel roles are confirmed, not assumed: from the single-line diagram (BFGEYD v1.2 PDF 4), the current-sharing figure of FR3D23 v1.0 PDF 8, and a Kirchhoff closure on the measured currents.

Done when the record docs/research/tf-cold-test-discharges.html tabulates every discharge with its trigger time, initial current, coil, FFS leg, CPC charge voltage (from the capacitor-side voltages before the trigger), the record times t0–t8, and the raw sample spacing (12.5 µs, read from the stamps), and gives each channel's confirmed role and scaling. Checks:

  • Positive: the current closure at the FDU node (for example resistor plus main-CCU current against the DC-line current, as the diagram fixes it) holds to within the 1.3 % spread mctb measured between current sensors, on every discharge after transfer.
  • Negative: a read of a window with no discharge (1 h before TF17-1_FD/1) returns the off-pulse baseline on every channel. A read of a name that does not exist is reported as a refusal, never as zeros.
  • MCCU:DV10 and EFD:DV7 are either given a scaling, checked against an independent quantity, or marked dead with the evidence.

Loader src/power_convertor/cold_test_data.py, tests tests/test_cold_test_data.py (on a synthetic store, never the archive), fetch scripts/mctb/fetch_discharges.py, shared capture helper scripts/iter/uda/capture.py with its three existing callers (save_pf_window.py, dummy_load_sessions.py, dummy_load_windows.py), data /home/ITER/mcintos/Code/power_convertor/data/mctb, record docs/research/tf-cold-test-discharges.html.

A store-augmentation node closes the section. Three nodes have landed: the discharge store (merge 5ef491e5), the QD store (402f4b45) and the store follow-ons (6cce65f1). The node cold-test-store-augmentation adds the windows later sections need, and closes the follow-ons the reviews left:

  • Windows, through the same fetch and layout: every hold plateau on both coils, not only the matched currents; EFD:DV7 at every flat top beside PC:DV3; and one supply-off window per coil after a discharge has decayed, with PC:DV3 and the QD channels, for §10's negative check.
  • Loader: available_windows lists only windows, so a non-window file such as line-coefficients.npz is never offered as one. Audit each RAW channel's role against the single-line diagram and a Kirchhoff closure, and record the result in the record's role table.
  • Writers: extract one atomic npz writer into src/power_convertor/cache.py, with cached_array keeping its schema and its rows, and make cold_test_data's writer a caller of it. Give capture.save_reply a receipt-only option for arrays the store's writer has already written, with its three callers unchanged.
  • Tests: compare the sidecar channel and archive names against independent literals rather than the fixture's own constant, and add a nonfinite latest prefire CPC sample to guard the last-finite behaviour.

Done when the new windows are in the store with their sidecars, the loader and writers carry the changes above with their tests, and the record lists the new windows and the role audit. Checks: Positive: cached_array returns the same arrays and keys as at the base revision. Negative: renaming the fixture's archive constant to a wrong name fails the sidecar test, and removing the finite-value filter fails the prefire test.

§3 — The commutation, measured

Before any model, measure what the commutation did on every discharge, from §2's raw windows. The S3 coordinator has asked for these quantities as the validation input for the ITER FDU commutation model (coil-circuit-playback-figures §8), so they are delivered first and on their own:

  • The sequence: BPS opening and the current's move to the VCB; the VCB command and opening; CPC firing; the VCB current zero; transfer to the resistor; and the late event near 1.5 s. Each is taken from the waveforms and set beside the controller's record time.
  • The CPC ring: its peak current, its period, and its decay, from the main-CCU and backup-CCU currents and the capacitor-side voltages.
  • The breaker's current zero against CPC firing, tzero − tCPC, and how it moves with coil current.
  • The arc voltage of each of the two series vacuum breakers through opening and current zero, from the per-VCB arc-voltage sensors (most likely MCCU:DV10–DV13; establish which is which, and note that DV10 read zero on the 30 kA shot). Report whether the two share the voltage and whether one ideal VCB is an adequate model at current zero.
  • The resistor and snubber transient: the resistor's voltage excursion and current reversal, their duration, and the fastest dv/dt the sampling resolves, stated as a lower bound on the true rate.
  • The coil-terminal and ground voltages through the transfer, against the ±92 V operating limit and the 4.1 kV specification.
  • The voltage spike at FDU opening that the lessons-learnt report attributes to the CPC (FRZHBR v1.0 p. 16): its size, timing and duration on every channel that shows it, including the quench-detection signals of §10. The ITER model's snubber-removed control arms produce such a spike from ideal valve turn-off, so a measured size and timing anchors it.

Then identify the CPC from the four zero-current discharges (TF17-1_ZC_FD/1–4). With only 35 A in the coil, the ring is the CPC discharging into the breaker loop alone, so its period and peak fix L and C, and its decay fixes the loop resistance. The ring current is read as MCCU:LA6 − MCCU:LA7 once the BPS has opened (§1's channel map), and the CPC charge is the 1.5–1.8 kV the store records before each September shot. Fit those three values with an interval from the spread between the four shots. The current discharges are then not used to fit anything here; they are held out for §4's prediction.

Done when the record docs/research/tf-cold-test-commutation.html tabulates, per discharge, every quantity above with the log or array it was read from, and gives the zero-current fit of the CPC's L, C and R with intervals. Its figure (rendered and inspected) shows the measured currents of the TF17 30 kA commutation on a few-millisecond window, with each event marked. Checks:

  • Positive: an LC ring with the fitted values, started at the measured charge voltage, reproduces each zero-current shot's measured ring current to within its own scatter.
  • Negative: the same fit with C halved misses the measured ring period by the factor √2 it must.
  • The measured current zero is compared with the analytic instant arcsin(I0√(L/C)/V)/ω computed from the fitted L and C. The record says how far it moves, which is the effect that fdu-breaker-current-zero addresses on the ITER model.

Send the table, with the CPC fit, to the S3 coordinator (power-convertor-81) the session it lands. Caller scripts/mctb/commutation_measured.py, record docs/research/tf-cold-test-commutation.html, figures docs/figures/tf-cold-test-commutation.

§4 — The FDU in the library, predicting the commutation

The FDU commutation circuit was first written in a script, scripts/iter/switched_discharge_insertion.py, on power_convertor.switched_circuit.Circuit. Its stamp and measured-zero solve now live in the library (merge e6b87224), and the script keeps simulate_fdu, fdu_current_zero_s, _fdu_lumped_circuit and _fdu_plant_circuit as callers. The library's former fast-discharge insertion, ConverterNetwork.add_fast_discharge, was a resistor bypass with no counter-pulse, snubber or resistor stray. The lift, now landed, put the commutation into one library owner, src/power_convertor/fast_discharge_unit.py, so that the ITER units and the test unit are built from the same code:

  • An FDU description: the BPS; a series string of n vacuum breakers, each with its own opening and arc-voltage model (n = 1 reproduces today's ideal VCB, n = 2 is the test unit); the CPC (L, C, charge voltage, thyristor); the backup breaker with its stray inductance; the snubber (R, C, stray L); and the resistor as §6's discharge_resistor element. The snubber's attachment is a parameter, never hard-coded: either across the FDU terminals, as the ITER builder and 7JQSNL place it, or across the main CCU in series with the backup breaker, as the test unit and XK23KG place it, where its loop carries the backup breaker's stray. The ITER rows keep their present placement, so they do not move. The S3 coordinator compares the two placements on the ITER rows once this owner exists.
  • A stamp onto a Circuit, and a two-pass solve that opens the breaker at its own measured branch current zero, as fdu-breaker-current-zero establishes. This section is gated on that node merging, below.
  • switched_discharge_insertion.py becomes a caller of the library, with its rows agreeing with the base revision to a relative 1e-9.
  • The library's existing owner, ConverterNetwork.add_fast_discharge (converter_units.py, returning a ProtectionFragment), becomes a delegate of the new module. A resistor bypass is the FDU description with its counter-pulse, snubber and stray omitted, so there is one fast-discharge owner, not two. Its callers keep their interface and their rows, to a relative 1e-9 against the base revision: scripts/iter/vs1_discharge.py, scripts/iter/converter_units.py, scripts/iter/fast_discharge.py and tests/test_converter_units.py. converter_units.py is held by the S3 coordinator's vs3-anti-series node at the time of writing. The edit waits for that claim to release, which the dispatch scope check enforces.

Then build the test FDU on the test circuit. The coil is the lumped 0.35 H with §5's posterior passive mode, which is why §4 waits on §5; the DC link has the inductance and resistance the data give. The CPC is §3's zero-current fit. The test FDU is built with the topology of the lead's Figure 17. The main CCU has four parallel branches (the BPS; two VCBs in series; the CPC; the RC snubber), in series with the pyrobreaker, and that pair sits in parallel with the 5 mΩ resistor. The snubber and resistor stray are stated assumptions, each run at both ends of a stated range, because their values are not held. Run both snubber placements, and report which one the measured commutation supports. Run every current discharge from the BPS opening to 20 ms after transfer and predict, without refitting: tzero − tCPC, the CPC peak, the transfer time, the resistor voltage excursion and current reversal, and the coil-terminal and ground voltages. Report each prediction's deviation from §3's measurement, and how much of it the snubber range spans.

Done when the library and its tests land, the ITER rows of switched_discharge_insertion.py and of every add_fast_discharge caller agree with the base revision to a relative 1e-9 in the gate log, and the record gives each current discharge's predicted and measured commutation quantities side by side, with a figure overlaying predicted and measured currents on the TF17 30 kA and TF07 10 kA commutations (rendered and inspected). Checks:

  • Positive: the library reproduces the lumped and sectioned-plant FDU rows of switched_discharge_insertion.py, read from the files fdu-breaker-current-zero merges (its repair round extends CS1's window to about 3 ms and restates the to-ground comparisons), to rounding. The control values are taken from the merged rows at the gate, never from earlier messages. Use PF2's rows. The check is that the library reproduces each merged PF2 row, lumped and plant, across and to ground, with and without the snubber, to a relative 1e-9 against that same row. It is not that the lumped and plant rows agree with each other. They agree to 0.2 % only on the across voltage with the snubber fitted (4233.2 V against 4241.3 V); their to-ground peaks differ by 2.3–2.5 %, and the snubber-removed row by 45 %. Those are properties of the two models, which the lift must preserve, not tolerances for the lift. Do not use CS1's: CS1 has two FDUs, one per module (778SPD v1.0 PDF 37–38, 43–48; 33CUHD v3.5 PDF 4), and the builder's single-FDU CS1 rows are being recomposed by the S3 coordinator's cs1-two-fdu node. The test facility's single coil has one FDU, so this difference does not arise in the cold-test circuit.
  • Negative: with the counter-pulse removed, the breaker branch never reaches zero and the solve reports a failed commutation instead of a transfer.
  • Negative: delaying the model's current zero by 0.1 ms moves its observable zero-after-onset outside the 0.05 ms acceptance on the TF17 30 kA record. The check first written here, that opening at the analytic instant shifts the transfer by §3's 0.16 ms, compared a physical zero with a filtered one; the result below explains why it was replaced.

Library src/power_convertor/fast_discharge_unit.py, tests tests/test_fast_discharge_unit.py, caller scripts/mctb/commutation_model.py; the edit to scripts/iter/switched_discharge_insertion.py waits for the gate, and the delegation in src/power_convertor/converter_units.py (with tests/test_converter_units.py) waits for its current claim to release. The record extends docs/research/tf-cold-test-commutation.html by splicing in a model section; figures docs/figures/tf-cold-test-commutation-model.

The first prediction landed on 20 October 2026, and its physical result is negative. The library owner (merge e6b87224) and the test FDU (merge 1fcc10f3) are on main. The shared FDU builds two series VCBs, §3's CPC, §5's passive mode, §6's resistor and both snubber placements. Of 360 sensitivity arms, 358 commutate, and the PF2 rows, the caller arrays and the protection rows are preserved exactly. The prediction disagrees with the measurement in four ways, each now diagnosed:

  • Timing. The declared check compared the model's physical current zero with §3's filtered observable. §3's measurement operator (a 21-sample mean, a sustained-low-current criterion and an onset threshold) adds about 0.14 ms. So §3's "0.16 ms after the analytic instant" is mostly the operator, not the breaker. Through the same operator, the model's zero after onset is 0.516 ms against 0.485 ms measured on TF17 at 30 kA. In that space, opening at the analytic instant and opening at the branch zero cannot be told apart.
  • Peaks. The model's CPC peak is 36.2 kA, an instantaneous maximum, against 42.8 kA measured as a 21-sample mean. Its coil-voltage peak is 655–2894 V against 252 V. The coil-voltage excess grows with the resistor stray inductance, assumed at 30 µH (10–100 µH), where GJ4JX4's circuit model gives 5 µH for the FDR cable. And the coil voltage DV9 is acquired at 1 kHz (GJ4JX4 p. 30), so the 252 V cannot bound a sub-millisecond peak.
  • Prefire state. At 30 kA the measured traces carry about 8 kA in the resistor before the CPC fires, and about 6 of 10 kA on TF07. The VCBs open 6–14 ms before firing (GJ4JX4 pp. 24, 27), and their arcs divert current; the model started with all of it in the VCBs.
  • Numerics. Once both series VCBs open, the joint between them is referenced only through open switches. The exact integrator then gives about 3×10¹² V, while the companion method stays finite.

A second node, cold-test-commutation-observables, completes the section:

  • Compare in observable space. Pass every predicted quantity through the operator of the channel it is compared with: its sample rate, averaging, onset and zero criteria, and DV9's 1 kHz acquisition. Report physical and observable values side by side. The timing acceptance is per record, the model's observable zero-after-onset against the measured one, with the TF17 30 kA record within 0.05 ms. That tolerance was set after the first result, so it is a consistency check; the delayed-zero control above is what makes it falsifiable.
  • Take the circuit inductances from GJ4JX4 v1.2 p. 29 as nominal: busbar 35 µH, FDR cable 5 µH, CPC 20 + 5 µH. Keep the earlier ranges as sensitivity arms, and compare the CPC-loop sum with §3's 31.3 µH fit rather than refitting it.
  • Start each record from the measured opening. The VCBs open 6–14 ms before firing, with the arc voltage taken from the measured VCB arc channels (DV11, DV13) where they resolve it, and GJ4JX4's 200 V model parameter as the stated prior where they do not. The measured prefire split between the breakers and the resistor is then a check, not a fit.
  • Reference the series-VCB joint physically, with a grading element per breaker, sourced or stated as an assumption, so the exact integrator is finite on the test circuit. Pass an integrator keyword through solve() with its default unchanged, unless the S3 coordinator's cs1-two-fdu node has added it first.
  • Predict the eight TF07 records labelled as current discharges that the 1 kA cut left out, or state per record why one cannot be predicted.
  • Build the earthing with ConverterNetwork.add_grounding rather than three hand-placed resistors, and make the charge test call make_case with the alternate charge.

Report which snubber placement the observable-space comparison supports, or that it still cannot tell them apart.

§5 — The coil's passive response: a prior from the structure, updated by the data

mctb fits one passive mode to the first 4 s of eight discharges: k² = 0.80, τ2 = 0.49 s, a 0.68 % fast drop, matched by the winding-pack helium heat. That mode is now the ITER model's conductor coupling (winding_losses). Here, test it as this repository's rules require a damping to be held: a sourced prior, updated by data, with both reported. The prior comes from the structure. The IDM single-coil-test analyses (FE6Y2R, 8Y627Y, 932C7C, GK8E9C) predict the energy each passive structure absorbs in an MCTB fast discharge. Their values and pages are recorded in the IDM table this plan carries, and the brief gives them; a worker never searches IDM. By mctb's equation (9) each predicted energy fixes a coupling b = E2/(½L1I0²). The robust sourced quantity is the coupled energy fraction b = E2/(½L1I0²). The analyses' 1 ms (radial plates) and 10 ms (case) are the coil current's response times, the fast coupled time τf = τ2(1 − k²) of mctb's equation (8), not each structure's own L/R. Read as L/R, they would force k² far above one. GK8E9C's 60 s energies give b ≈ 0.81 % at 10 kA for case and plates together, carried as 0.5–1.2 % because the measured winding-pack heat came out 40 % above the calculation. With τf log-uniform over 1–10 ms, equation (8) gives k² ≈ 0.96–0.995 and τ2 ≈ 0.2–0.3 s. Two independent modes cannot both carry k² near one, so the structure enters as one effective mode, and a slower conductor-coupling mode (mctb's 98 ms) is admitted if the data need it. nova's held export carries no TF case or plates. The values below were read through Lucy on 20 October 2026, on printed report pages.

The prior and mctb's fit already disagree in a way this section must settle. The analyses place the structure's response at about 1 ms for the plates and 10 ms for the case. mctb's single mode has a fast time constant of 98 ms, with τ2 = 0.49 s. Yet the energies roughly agree: mctb's mode deposits about 0.12 MJ at 10 kA, against the analyses' 0.14 MJ for case and plates in a 60 s discharge. The 80 kHz data resolve a 1 ms transient, while mctb's fit used 0.5 ms averages beginning after the transfer. So the first test is whether a millisecond-scale drop is present in the raw current, hidden inside the commutation window. Energy deposited by a slow discharge scales with dI/dt, so the analyses at 5 s are rescaled to the measured 60 s decays by their L/R, not compared directly.

Fit the measured fast transient as mctb did, from §2's raw and envelope data: the current's shortfall below the resistive decay over the first 4 s, on every current discharge of both coils. Do it for one mode and for two, the second with the case's slower time constant. mctb found 0.13–0.46 MJ of casing heat with no resolved transient, and the ITER TF discharge model (scripts/iter/tf_fast_discharge.py) carries an assumed 20 s case mode, sized to bring the resistor energy within 778SPD's limit. The cold test is the only measurement that can bound that mode. Report the prior, the data-updated values with intervals, how far the data moved them, and the largest slow case coupling the data allow at 20 s, with its effect on τ.

Done when the record docs/research/tf-cold-test-passive-mode.html states for each mode the prior (value, interval, source), the posterior, and the bound on a 20 s case mode. Its figure, rendered and inspected, shows the measured fast drop on both coils against the prior and the posterior. Checks:

  • Positive: the posterior reproduces mctb's 0.68 % at 98 ms within its interval.
  • Negative: with the passive mode removed, the model misses the measured first-4 s shortfall by its full 0.68 %.
  • Negative: the fraction is independent of current across 5–30 kA. A model that scales the drop with I₀, as hysteresis loss would, is rejected by the data, and the record states by how much.

The structure's decay modes already have a library owner, and this section extends it rather than fitting modes beside it. PassiveStructure (src/power_convertor/passive_structure.py) gives modes() from the nova matrices and fit_scales; PassiveLoopModel and fit_loops are in passive_loops.py; the exporter is scripts/iter/nova_passive_matrices.py. The cold-test mode (k², τ2 referred to the coil) is the coil-referred reduction of those modes. Where PassiveStructure lacks that reduction, add it there. The prior then comes from the structure's own L/R where nova provides the TF case and radial plates, and from the IDM analyses otherwise. Caller scripts/mctb/passive_mode.py, any extension in src/power_convertor/passive_structure.py with its tests, record docs/research/tf-cold-test-passive-mode.html, figures docs/figures/tf-cold-test-passive-mode.

§6 — The resistor's heating and its resistance law

Two copies of the energy-linear law already exist. scripts/iter/fast_discharge.py (resistor_slope_ohm_per_j) and scripts/iter/tf_fast_discharge.py each set R = R0 + kFE for the ITER units from 778SPD's rise factor. mctb measures kF on the test resistor. Move the law into one library element, src/power_convertor/discharge_resistor.py, with an adiabatic heat balance. Its state is absorbed energy and element temperature, and it gives resistance from temperature through the material's α and cp, both temperature-dependent where data give them. Fan cooling between discharges uses a thermal resistance. The energy-linear law is then the constant-cp, constant-α limit, not a separate model. Both ITER scripts call it, with their rows unchanged to rounding.

Test it on the cold test. From §2's data, form R = VFDR/IFDR against absorbed energy within each of the ten current discharges, after the baseline correction mctb found necessary at low voltage. Set it beside the element's prediction, made from the stainless slices' material data and the module resistance from CURR44 v1.2 (29.1 mΩ at 4 °C, 29.75 mΩ at 20 °C). Note that the conversion between those two readings implies the α the factory used. Read the starting temperature from the FDU air sensors and the cooling between discharges, and test whether the element predicts the next discharge's starting resistance from the previous one's energy. Where the data distinguish shapes of R(E) (energy-linear, or curved through cp(T) and α(T)), say so, because the ITER peak voltage depends on that shape between 778SPD's endpoints (tf_fast_discharge.py carries p = ½, 1 and 2 as cases).

Done when the record docs/research/tf-cold-test-resistor.html gives the measured kF beside the element's prediction from material data, the inferred element mass and α with intervals, the predicted starting resistance of each discharge against the measured value, and which R(E) shapes the data exclude over the measured rise (up to about +54 K). Its figure shows R against E for all discharges, with the element's prediction; it is rendered and inspected. Checks:

  • Positive: the element reproduces mctb's kF = 1.83 ± 0.13 µΩ/MJ within the interval.
  • Negative: an element with α = 0 predicts a constant resistance, and the measured 30 kA discharge rejects it by its measured rise.
  • The ITER rows of fast_discharge.py and tf_fast_discharge.py agree with their values before the change to a relative 1e-9, or to the scripts' printed precision where a row is printed. The pre-change values are captured at the node's base revision and compared in its gate log.

Library src/power_convertor/discharge_resistor.py, tests tests/test_discharge_resistor.py, caller scripts/mctb/resistor_heating.py, record docs/research/tf-cold-test-resistor.html, figures docs/figures/tf-cold-test-resistor. The law has five consumers, not two. One of them is §4's FDU description, which takes the resistor as this element, so §4 waits on this section. Besides fast_discharge.py and tf_fast_discharge.py, scripts/iter/tf_supply_circuit.py calls tf_fast_discharge.calibrate_k_f, applies with_k_f and publishes slope_ohm_per_j. scripts/figures/arc_fast_discharge.py reads fast_discharge.RESISTOR_RISE_FACTOR and FDU_RESISTANCE_OHM. The names those consumers read (resistor_slope_ohm_per_j, calibrate_k_f, with_k_f, RESISTOR_RISE_FACTOR, FDU_RESISTANCE_OHM) keep their shapes and become delegations to the library element. All four consumers' outputs are checked unchanged to the same 1e-9 tolerance in the gate log. The edits to the two ITER scripts are confined to replacing their law with the library call.

§7 — The whole discharge replayed, and the voltage to ground

Assemble the test circuit from the parts the earlier sections validated and replay every discharge from the trigger to 480 s, fitting nothing to the slow decay:

  • the converter's 100 ms inversion at 140° and its blocking;
  • the FFS, with the TFFS thyristor drop on TF07 and the mechanical leg on TF17;
  • §4's FDU and §5's passive mode;
  • §6's resistor, from its measured starting temperature;
  • the warm loop with its measured resistance;
  • the EFD earthing network with BFGEYD's resistors, built through the library's existing earthing owner rather than a new description. ConverterNetwork.add_grounding (converter_units.py) already builds the terminal resistors to a neutral and the neutral-to-earth resistor, with optional shunt capacitors and a leakage source. It has no element a contactor inserts, so this section extends it with one: an optional resistor that a contactor inserts in the neutral-to-earth path, absent by default. Every existing caller's rows stay unchanged to rounding, and the extension carries its own test. The EFD's 9840 Ω member then has a place in the same owner. The edit to converter_units.py and tests/test_converter_units.py waits for any live claim on them to release. winding_losses.EarthUnit, ripple_margins.CircuitGround and filter_network.GroundingSystem are the other existing descriptions; the record says which the replay used and why. That reuse is what makes the measured ground voltage a test of the ITER method rather than of a parallel model of it.

Compare the current, the resistor voltage, the full-coil voltage (EQDD1/2:FC_V_D) and the voltage to ground with the measurements, using mctb's measures (80–10 % τ and waveform rms as a percentage of I₀) and the 778SPD measure τeq = 2∫I²dt/I₀². The voltage to ground is the second transferable result. The ITER TF model obtains it from the documented earthing network, terminal resistors to a neutral and that neutral to earth through 1 kΩ (778SPD pp. 101–105). The test circuit has the same structure at 271 Ω, 990 Ω and 9840 Ω. The measured ground voltage and the per-discharge peak records test that method directly.

Done when the record docs/research/tf-cold-test-replay.html tabulates for every discharge the measured and replayed τ, τeq and waveform rms, and the measured and replayed peak voltages to ground, with each contribution switched on in turn as mctb's table does. Its figure, rendered and inspected, shows measured and replayed current and ground voltage for one discharge of each coil. Checks:

  • Positive: the replay matches mctb's waveform rms (0.04–0.27 %) or the record explains each discharge where it does not.
  • Negative: with the EFD divider removed and the circuit grounded at one terminal, the replayed ground voltage departs from the measurement by the factor the balanced divider removes.
  • Negative: with TF07's freewheeling path given the mechanical leg instead of the thyristor drop, the replayed τ at 1 kA departs from the measurement by the 19 s mctb attributes to the drop.

§8 — The test converter and its ripple, TF07 against TF17

mctb measured the flat-top coil-voltage ripple at about 7 times TF17's at equal current: 2.1–2.8 V at 25–50 Hz on TF07, against 0.32–0.72 V at 100 Hz on TF17. Neither campaign's ripple is at the 12-pulse line (600 Hz) a balanced supply puts first. Two causes are on record and they predict different spectra. FR3D23 reports two independent PI loops sharing one coil with no balancing, and warns of voltage oscillations from bridge imbalance. FYXJSN measured a 12.5 Hz flat-top oscillation on TF07, and a ±8 V full-circuit oscillation, which it attributes to the current loop. A loop interaction of that kind sits at a few tens of hertz, set by the gains and the bridges' shared inductance. The lead reports that a filter was needed for TF17. A filter acts at the ripple lines and leaves its resonance in the converter-to-coil transfer. First measure, from §2's flat-top and ramp windows:

  • the spectra of the converter voltage (PC:DV3), the DC-line voltages and the full-coil voltage on both coils, at matched current;
  • the transfer from converter voltage to coil voltage, which shows whether a filter's resonance appears between TF07 and TF17;
  • the per-bridge currents, if §2 found them archived.

A first read of EQDD1 on 20 October 2026, over 60 s of flat top, gives the spectra the model must meet. On TF07 at 5 and 10 kA, FC_V carried 2.6 and 2.2 V rms, led by 25.05–25.07 Hz with harmonics at 50 Hz. On TF17 at 10 and 30 kA, it carried 0.38 and 0.73 V rms, led by 100 Hz with 50 and 300 Hz (§10 gives the table). Two features matter. TF07's lines sit at exact subharmonics of the mains, 50/2 Hz here and 50/4 and 50/3 Hz in FYXJSN. A linear PI–plant oscillation would sit at a frequency set by the gains, not locked to 50/n, so the hypothesis to test is a limit cycle of the loop with the mains-synchronous firing, aggravated by the two bridge loops hunting against each other. TF17's 50 and 100 Hz lines are not characteristic of a 12-pulse supply, and point instead to asymmetry inside the one unit that ran: unequal firing or interphase-reactor imbalance between its two star groups, or supply or transformer unbalance. On TF17 there was no second unit to be unequal with. Then model the test converter with the library's thyristor bridges rather than a new one. bridge.BridgeSet and CirculatingBridgeGroup give two 6-pulse bridges with an interphase reactor on delta and star transformers, and current_control gives one PI loop per bridge with FR3D23's gains. The load is the 0.35 H coil and the DC link. Reproduce TF07's 25–50 Hz lines with both units in parallel, each with its own PI loop. Then change only what changed for TF17, which was running one unit with one loop and no filter (§1), and predict TF17's spectrum: the uncancelled 300 Hz line, the 100 and 50 Hz lines and the absence of the loop line. The 50 and 100 Hz lines need a modelled cause, because a balanced 6-pulse unit produces neither. Carry each unit's asymmetry as stated parameters: a firing-angle offset between its two star groups, an interphase-reactor imbalance, and a supply negative-sequence fraction. Identify them on TF07, whose own 50 and 100 Hz lines (2.38 and 1.85 V at 10 kA) fix them per unit, and carry them unchanged to TF17's single unit. Which unit ran on TF17 is not recorded, so run both and report each. A further check: with the asymmetry parameters set to zero, the TF17 prediction loses its 50 and 100 Hz lines, so those rows of the prediction are falsifiable. The §1 table gives the measured amplitudes both predictions are judged against. Compare both spectra with the 0.1 % (68 A) ripple requirement as a current. This is the same method the JT-60SA filter prediction used (filter-grounding-prediction): parameters fixed on the first campaign, the second predicted from the documented change alone.

Done when the record docs/research/tf-cold-test-converter.html gives the measured TF07 and TF17 spectra and transfers, names which mechanism the data support (with the line and transfer evidence), and gives the model's TF07 reproduction and TF17 prediction line by line, with deviations in dB. Its figure, rendered and inspected, shows both measured spectra with the model's. Checks:

  • Positive: the balanced 12-pulse model with balanced bridges puts its first ripple line at 600 Hz, at the amplitude bridge.mean_voltage and the commutation reactance give.
  • Negative: with the two PI loops replaced by one loop on the coil current, the 25–50 Hz line falls below the measured TF07 level, or the record says it does not, and that the loop interaction is then not the cause.
  • Negative: putting the second unit back into the TF17 model, with its own PI loop, cancels the 300 Hz line and restores a TF07-like loop line at tens of hertz. If it does not, the record says the single-unit reading is not what changed.

The validated converter model, with its firing, control cycle and parallel-bridge loops, is the open-loop model §11 designs on, so the record states its validation explicitly: which lines and transfers it reproduces, and to what accuracy. Caller scripts/mctb/converter_ripple.py, record docs/research/tf-cold-test-converter.html, figures docs/figures/tf-cold-test-converter. A new library element is added only where bridge, current_control or filter_network cannot express the test converter, and the record says why.

Result, 20 October 2026: the spectra are measured and the model is not validated. The spectra node (merge 0828e8a4) gives the lines in §1's table: TF07's 25 Hz loop line at 1.95 V and TF17's 300 Hz line at 6.37 V, with no added filter on either coil. The model node (merge 0ad30ea3) is a negative result. Its three-parameter two-unit fit leaves a 75.5 V-equivalent residual. Its single-unit prediction misses TF17's 50 and 100 Hz lines by 19–24 dB, and a gain scale of 22 fails on the held-out records. Its four measured-accuracy tests are enabled and fail, so the miss stays visible in the suite. The constants a validated model needs, namely the commutation and interphase reactances, the gain units and the firing limits, are not in accessible IDM. So on 20 October 2026 the lead decided that §11 designs over an envelope of them instead. TF17 ran on one converter unit with no added filter (decision tf17-filter-values).

§9 — What transfers to the ITER model, and to whom

Write the synthesis docs/research/tf-cold-test-synthesis.html. For each validated method (commutation at the breaker's own zero, the snubber and resistor transient, the passive mode, the resistor law and its shape, the earthing-network ground voltage, and the parallel-bridge converter control), it gives the measured deviation and the uncertainty the method carries into the ITER model, as an interval the ITER results can take. It also says which owner takes each result:

  • coil-circuit-playback-figures §8, or its follow-on: §3's measured commutation and §4's prediction;
  • scripts/iter/tf_fast_discharge.py: the bound on the 20 s case mode, which replaces an assumption, and the R(E) shape evidence;
  • winding_losses: the posterior passive mode in place of the bare fit;
  • the ITER TF converter: FR3D23's balancing finding, §8's result and §11's controller method, which apply to any parallel-bridge supply;
  • quench-detection-converter-pickup: §10's measured transfers, rejection ratios, the FDU-opening spike and the aliasing finding, as validation controls for its detector and its co-wound-tape element;
  • the facility's operators, through the lead: §11's recommended controllers for the next TF and PF1 tests;
  • the model claims register.

Each is delivered as a followup on its owning plan or a message to its coordinator, not as an edit to another plan's files from here.

Done when the synthesis is written with its figure (one panel per validated method, measured against predicted, rendered and inspected), every transfer above names its owning plan and the followup or message that carries it, and scripts/iter/tf_fast_discharge.py's cold-test reproduction (cold_test_circuit) is rebuilt from this plan's parameters rather than mctb's constants, with its rows unchanged to within the stated intervals. Negative control: rebuilt with mctb's bare constants in place of this plan's posteriors (k² 0.80, τ2 0.49 s, kF 1.83 µΩ/MJ, no FDU stray), the cold-test reproduction must fall outside at least one of the stated intervals. If it does not, the record says that this plan's measurements did not move the model, and the transfer to the ITER owners is stated as a confirmation, not an update. Record docs/research/tf-cold-test-synthesis.html (its own slug, so it does not collide with this plan's), figures docs/figures/tf-cold-test-validation.

§10 — Quench detection on the test coils: what reached the detector, and the margin left

The TF coils carry two detection paths, and the cold tests archive both, per double pancake, on two redundant chains (EQDD1 and EQDD2). The values below were read through Lucy on 20 October 2026.

ElectronicsTwo identical EQDD chains (1-out-of-2), CompactRIO discrimination synchronous on a 1 ms cycle, discharge-request vote 2-out-of-3. Conditioner ranges ±30 V (DP taps), ±10 V (CWT), ±500 V (RP). A 30 Hz low-pass with −40 dB/decade sits on the QD acquisition; a 10 Hz filter was proposed for the tokamak5U6PVV v2.3 pp. 2, 8, 12–15, 20; FYXJSN v1.0 pp. 5–6; FXW4SY v1.0 p. 14
CriteriaBusbars 10 mV, HTS legs 1 mV, HX legs 60 mV, full circuit 1000 mV (later removed as unusable), all at 1.5 s. TF DP RT-pair and CWT-pair comparisons 100 mV at 1.5 s, marked TBD. FYXJSN evaluated against 30 mV. The 2012 ITER design gives 100 mV and 1 s5U6PVV v2.3 p. 19; FRZHBR v1.0 p. 10; FYXJSN v1.0 p. 6; D7C5PC v1.2 p. 7
PredictionsAt 10 kA and 60 s: a compensated spike of 0.38 V decaying in about 10 ms (passive structure, mostly the radial plates), on a 10.2 mV baseline. Measured TF07 spikes were 120 mV central and 40 mV edge, 2–3 times lower than predicted, possibly limited by bandwidthE5JNHZ v1.1 pp. 2, 4; GPE7WS v1.0 pp. 7–10; FXW4SY v1.0 pp. 12–13

The TF07 noise is documented (FYXJSN v1.0 pp. 4–6). At 10 kA the flat top carried ±7 mV on the CWT-compensated pairs and ±300 mV on the RT pairs. Against a 30 mV threshold, that means a quench would be asserted only at 37 mV on the CWT pairs and about 330 mV on the RT pairs. A read of EQDD1 on 20 October 2026 (60 s of flat top before each discharge) gives this comparison at matched current:

TF07 5 kATF07 10 kATF17 10 kATF17 30 kA
FC_V rms and strongest lines2.57 V; 25.07 Hz (2.8 V)2.15 V; 25.05 and 50.08 Hz0.38 V; 100, 300 and 50 Hz0.73 V; 100 and 50 Hz
DP42_RT_V peak-to-peak317 mV246 mV48 mV62 mV
DP42_CW_V peak-to-peak14.5 mV14.6 mV6.3 mV8.3 mV

So the RT-pair noise fell by about 5 times from TF07 to TF17, and its frequency moved from the 25 Hz loop line to 50 and 100 Hz. On TF17 the CWT pairs are clean. The RT pairs still peak near 30 mV, comparable to the threshold FYXJSN used but inside the specification's 100 mV. FRZHBR's entry "converter ripple blinded real-time QD" was approved in August, before TF17, so it describes TF07. No document records the QD state on TF17.

Measure, from §2's whole-test QD windows and the 80 kHz supply channels at the same instants:

  • the transfer, magnitude and phase per frequency up to 500 Hz, from the converter voltage PC:DV3 to each DP's raw and compensated signal, at each flat top where the inductive term is steady;
  • the CWT rejection ratio per frequency and per DP (compensated over raw), central against edge;
  • the common-mode and differential split: the QD residual regressed jointly on the converter differential voltage and the earthing voltage EFD:DV7;
  • the FDU-opening spike from −50 ms to +200 ms on every DP and both chains, against the 80 kHz FDU branch voltages, beside E5JNHZ's 0.38 V prediction, and whether double compensation removes it as FXW4SY shows;
  • the detector front end, measured rather than assumed. Report the complex ratio QD/PC:DV3, magnitude and phase, per DP at each converter line (25, 50, 100, 300 and 600 Hz and the others present), for raw and compensated signals, on TF07 and TF17 at matched current. Fit it as the product of a winding transfer and a low-pass of free corner and order, and report both with intervals. TF07's 25 Hz-dominated drive against TF17's 300 Hz-dominated drive is the leverage for that fit. A result near 30 Hz and second order confirms 5U6PVV and FYXJSN; any other result is the first measured front end, which quench-detection-converter-pickup carries into PF and CS;
  • complex line coefficients: for every flat-top window, the PC:DV3, EFD:DV7 and QD lines as complex coefficients on one common time reference, written in one file beside the windows in the store and keyed by line frequency. That is the form DetectionSection takes (lines={f: c} with a measured line_transfer), and it makes phase-sensitive differential and common-mode separation possible;
  • aliasing: whether the 1 kHz archive is the CompactRIO's own 1 ms discrimination stream (5U6PVV pp. 12–13 says the host receives data every 1 ms), and what passes the front end. At 1 kHz, 600 Hz folds to 400, 900 to 100, 1200 to 200, 1500 to 500 and 3000 to dc. Test TF17's 304 Hz lines with their ±4 and ±8 Hz sidebands as 696 or 1304 Hz images against the 80 kHz PC:DV3 spectrum: a QD line at a frequency DV3 does not carry is the aliasing signature;
  • for the FDU-opening spike, keep the QD samples and the 80 kHz FDU branch voltages on one time base, so the edge, its transfer and the hold can be followed sample by sample.

The windows the quench-detection session asked for are written by §2, which owns the one store and its one layout. This section reads them through §2's loader, writes no data, and adds no store, layout or writer of its own. It sends their path to that session. This section measures and does not model the tape. The co-wound-tape element has one owner, quench-detection-converter-pickup §4, which adds it to coil_windings as a coil-agnostic element with CS first and TF second; no parallel element is built here.

Done when the record docs/research/tf-cold-test-quench-detection.html tabulates each item above per DP and per chain for both coils, with the fitted front-end corner and order and their intervals. The line-coefficient file is in the store. The margins to the thresholds are §12's, once the detector's second-order stage exists. Its figure shows the TF07 and TF17 flat-top spectra of an RT pair and a CWT pair at matched current, with the threshold, and is rendered and inspected. The windows are in place, and the quench-detection session (power-convertor-45) has their path. Checks:

  • Positive: the measured CWT rejection near 1 Hz, on ramp windows long enough to excite it, is within a factor of two of the documented 1000. The flat-top windows of the first node could not test this: their matched-window medians were 47, 68, 360 and 337.
  • Negative: the same transfer computed from a window with the supply off (after the discharge has decayed) has no coherence with PC:DV3 above the noise floor.
  • Negative: double compensation of two CWT-compensated DPs reduces the FDU-opening spike, as FXW4SY shows; where it does not, the record says so.

Caller scripts/mctb/quench_detection.py (reading §2's windows through cold_test_data), record docs/research/tf-cold-test-quench-detection.html, figures docs/figures/tf-cold-test-quench-detection.

That is close to the documented 30 Hz low-pass (5U6PVV; GJ4JX4 p. 39), but the intervals exclude 30 Hz. 3337 coherent cells pass the phase surrogate, and TF17's 304 Hz lines are not aliases (0 of 92). The line-coefficient file is in the store. A second node, cold-test-qd-cross-checks, measures what remains once §2's store augmentation adds EFD:DV7 at the flat tops and a supply-off window:

§11 — Current controllers for the next TF and the PF1 tests

One more TF coil and PF1 remain to be tested in the facility. PF1 is 0.70 H at up to 48 kA and 806 MJ, on the same converter and FDU ratings (9AVFZK v1.1 PDF 4). The TF07 record shows a controller tuned by hand during a single energisation. It used two independent PI loops, one per converter bridge, with no current-balancing loop, and its gains changed six times between tests. FR3D23 concludes that the final gains would serve 34 kA but not 68 kA, because bridge imbalance could take one bridge to its overcurrent limit (FR3D23 v1.0 PDF 11–14). Its proposed strategy is in Y4F4P7 v1.1 and TX2YGL v1.0. Design the controllers from models, rather than by hand on the coil.

The lead decided on 20 October 2026 how this section proceeds: a robust design plus an on-coil identification test. The reason is §8's negative result. The cold-test data cannot validate an open-loop converter model, because the constants it needs are not documented in accessible IDM. BKENDJ v1.6, the facility's control design report, confirms the structure:

  • two independent PI loops, one per converter unit, each comparing its own reference with its own current and commanding its unit's firing angle through a limiter and an angle-calculation block;
  • a fast-controller cycle of 100 µs;
  • a separate reference per unit, and no balancing loop (BKENDJ v1.6 PDF 16, 36–37).

It gives no gain units or per-unit bases, no firing-angle or rate limits, and no interphase-reactor or commutation reactance. The contractor's converter design reports (BKDB95, BGQMEU) are withheld from this account. GFTG3P slide 9 may give the transformer as 1200 kVA, 22 kV / 36.4 V, an unverified OCR reading. EAWV57 v1.1 reports only static current-sharing tests (PDF 91–105, 129–131). The section therefore delivers two things.

  • A robust design. Use the structure Y4F4P7 v1.1 proposes for the ITER TF circuit (PDF 4): an outer coil-current PI producing a DC voltage reference, one bridge following it, and a second PI driving the bridge-current imbalance to zero, with a constant margin angle in inversion. Keep the per-bridge independent loops of the as-built controller as the comparison. Express the gains in physical units: volts per ampere, and volts per ampere-second for the integral term. Carry each undocumented constant as a stated envelope: commutation reactance, interphase-reactor inductance, unit no-load voltage, firing delay and the gain scaling. Report phase and gain margins as their worst case over that envelope, not at one point. The envelope is bounded by what the cold tests did measure:
    • §8's spectra, including the 600 Hz amplitude that its balanced model reproduces;
    • §5's passive mode;
    • TF07's 25, 16.5 and 12.5 Hz loop lines under FR3D23's gains (P 15 / I 20 at 5 kA, P 7 / I 21 at 10 kA). The envelope must place the as-built loop at or beyond its stability boundary under those gains. Any part of the envelope that would make those gains comfortably stable is excluded by the data.
  • An identification protocol for the start of the next campaign. It covers small reference steps or a low-amplitude pseudo-random sequence on each unit, at low current with the coil connected, and the measurements to record. From those, the plant constants and the gain scaling follow, before the recommended gains are finalised. Give the test length, the excitation amplitude against the coil's voltage and current limits, the channels to record and the quench-detection noise it would cause.

Design with the library's discrete PI machinery, power_convertor.current_control (design_pi, sampled_closed_loop_margins, loop_margins, sample_hold_response), as scripts/iter/controller_loop_margins.py uses it for the ITER supplies. Extend it only where a parallel-bridge loop needs it:

  • a common coil-current loop with a separate bridge-current balancing loop, as Y4F4P7 proposes;
  • the per-bridge alternative kept as the comparison.

Targets are a phase margin of at least 45° (60° preferred) and a gain margin of at least 6 dB (10 dB preferred), measured on the sampled loop with the firing delay. The cases are:

  • the next TF coil at 34 kA, and at 68 kA for completeness;
  • PF1 at 48 kA and 0.70 H, with its own passive response as a stated prior (the stand-alone PF1 analyses, for example 9ALK99 v1.1, read by the coordinator into the brief);
  • ramps at 10 A/s, the accelerated discharge at 40 A/s, and the start-up from zero current that FR3D23 found overshooting.

Close each design in the switched converter model, with firing limits, and predict the flat-top QD noise against the 30 and 100 mV thresholds. Do this by passing the closed-loop converter spectrum, with §10's measured transfers and its measured front end, to ripple_margins.DetectionSection. This is the frequency-domain path through residual, whose analogue stage is DetectionSection.bandwidth_hz with analogue_order: set them to §10's fitted corner and order, so the front end is applied there exactly once, and pass §10's de-embedded winding transfer as line_transfer, not the measured QD/DV3 ratio. That stage belongs to quench-detection-converter-pickup, not to §12, and it is on main, so this section waits on neither.

Done when the record docs/research/tf-cold-test-controllers.html gives:

  • the envelope of undocumented constants, with how the TF07 loop lines bound it;
  • the identification protocol, ready for the facility's operators;
  • for each case, the recommended gains, the bridge-balancing loop, and the measured margins;
  • the closed-loop step and ramp responses, and the bridge current imbalance at 34, 48 and 68 kA;
  • the predicted QD noise against the thresholds.

Its figures show a Bode plot of the open loop at the recommended and TF07 gains with the margins marked, and the closed-loop flat-top QD noise for both, rendered and inspected. Checks:

  • Negative: with FR3D23's TF07 gains, every plant in the envelope is at or beyond its stability boundary, consistent with the observed limit cycle; an envelope in which those gains are comfortably stable is rejected.
  • Negative: with the balancing loop removed at 68 kA, the bridge imbalance grows past the per-bridge overcurrent limit, as FR3D23 warns.
  • Positive: the recommended gains meet both margin targets across the whole envelope in every case, and their predicted flat-top QD noise on the RT pairs falls below 30 mV through §10's measured front end (about 25 Hz, second order).

The record is a recommendation for the facility's operators. It goes to them through the lead, never directly from this repository. Caller scripts/mctb/current_controllers.py, record docs/research/tf-cold-test-controllers.html, figures docs/figures/tf-cold-test-controllers. Any library extension goes in src/power_convertor/current_control.py with its tests in tests/test_current_control.py, the ITER rows of controller_loop_margins.py unchanged.

§12 — Detection margins on the measured front end

With §10's measured transfers, front end and line coefficients in hand, compute each pancake pair's margin to the thresholds, for TF07 and TF17 at matched current. Take each pair's noise through ripple_margins.DetectionSection, whose second-order analogue stage and sampling before the recursion in hold_response are on main (commits cd2612b7 and b69af88d). The rest of what this section consumes came from quench-detection-converter-pickup §3, which closed at merge e554a9fd, all in DetectionSection: the per-line bridge transfer in place of the scalar imbalance, cascaded analogue stages, the recursive exponential filter at the sampling rate, and the time-domain dwell path in hold_response. The ripple lines use the per-line transfer; edges and hold checks use the dwell path. There are two paths, and each applies the front end exactly once. The line path is residual(lines, ground). Its lines are the stored PC:DV3 drive coefficients only, with the documented earthing impedances in CircuitGround, which takes impedances and no voltage. residual already forms a modelled common-mode term from that divider, so the measured term replaces it rather than adding to it. Pass line_transfer as a differential and common-mode pair. Its common weight is zero. Its differential weight is §10's winding transfer plus §10's regression coefficient on EFD:DV7 times the stored ratio of the EFD:DV7 line to the PC:DV3 line, so the measured common-mode term passes through the same front end, aliasing and hold. Report the modelled common-mode term beside the measured one as a check. If the QD session adds a measured-ground entry to residual, use that instead; the stored QD coefficients are what this path predicts, never an input to it. The winding transfer inside that pair's differential weight is §10's de-embedded transfer, the measured QD/DV3 ratio divided by §10's fitted low-pass. There is one line_transfer, the pair just described. Its analogue stage is set to §10's fitted corner and order, with sampling_hz=1000 and filter_tau_s swept for the recursion. margin() then gives threshold minus residual. The time-domain path is hold_response(signal, step_s, threshold_v) on the recorded 1 kHz QD samples of each flat-top window. Those samples have already passed the hardware front end and the 1 kHz sampling, so this path applies only the recursion, and it gives the longest dwell above each threshold. That needs the recursion-only mode of hold_response: no analogue stage, a stride of 1, and only the recursion and the dwell count. The detector's owner provides it. Call hold_response(signal, step_s, threshold_v, front_end_applied=True), which is on main and refuses a step_s other than the sampling period. Neither a patch to ripple_margins.py from here nor a re-implemented recursion in the caller is allowed. Use thresholds of 30 and 100 mV with a 1.5 s validation time. This section consumes the detector and never patches ripple_margins.py.

Done when the record docs/research/tf-cold-test-quench-detection.html gains a margins section. It states each pair's margin to 30 and 100 mV, per DP and per chain, for TF07 and TF17 at matched current. It reports the longest dwell above each threshold against the validation time. It names the converter line that sets each margin. Checks:

  • Positive: TF07's computed residual on the RT pairs reproduces FYXJSN's ±300 mV at 10 kA within the scatter between pairs.
  • Positive: on every flat-top window, two coherent forms of the same coefficients agree within the scatter between pairs. The first is the peak of the coherent sum of the line path's per-line complex outputs, |ΣAfeiωt| maximised over t, taken before residual sums magnitudes. residual exposes only the scalar, so compose Af in the caller from ripple_margins' public functions (analogue_response, aliased_frequency, recursion_response) with the same line transfer, and assert that 2Σ|Af| equals residual() to 1e-12. That assertion shows the composition is the owner's arithmetic, not a second implementation. The second is hold_response's peak on a time series synthesised from the same coefficients and passed through the analogue stage. A disagreement between them means the front end has been counted twice or not at all. The residual 2Σ|Af| is an envelope over line phases, so it bounds both, and the recorded samples' peak, from above. The record reports all three, and a recorded peak above the envelope is a finding.
  • Negative: with the converter lines replaced by their averaged voltage, the residual falls to the slow inductive imbalance alone, which the record states beside it.

Caller scripts/mctb/quench_detection.py (its margins step), record docs/research/tf-cold-test-quench-detection.html (a spliced section), figures docs/figures/tf-cold-test-quench-margins.

§13 — The FDR's transient inductance: the method on the cold test, the material per section for ITER

The lead approved this study on 21 October 2026, with one rule: ITER's FDUs are sized differently from the test unit, so what transfers is the material's behaviour per section, never one resistor's inductance. The ITER FDR section is common to TF, CS and PF (S9BRS4 v2.0 pp. 25–29): 145 cold-rolled mild-steel sheets, 580 mm × 1 mm, welded into a zigzag at 4 mm spacing, 110.59 m of conductor. The coils differ only in sections in parallel per module (CS 2, PF1 and PF6 3, PF2–PF5 and TF 4) and in modules in series (TF 18). 7LDTQA's table, which §4's library now accepts, is magnetostatic: OPERA-2D with μ(B), no eddy currents and no skin effect. One-millimetre steel sheets at millisecond rise times are where eddy currents matter.

The cold-test FDR is not that section. CURR44 v1.2 (pp. 8–9, 20–22) describes the MCTB FDR as stainless-steel slices with zigzag welds, silvered-copper terminals, mica insulation and a carbon-steel shell; each module is 29.1 mΩ at 4 °C. EALJ5A v1.0 tested nine modules. Their internal arrangement and the bus geometry are not documented in the accessible IDM (BFFVQS v3.0 lists the drawings only), and D9XWQ5's 5.45 mΩ is the circuit value, not a module's. So the cold test cannot give the mild-steel material behaviour. It gives two things:

  • The method, validated on a resistor of near-unit permeability. From the 80 kHz commutation windows, form the flux linkage λ(t) = ∫(vR − R(E)·i) dt, with vR on FDR:DV8, i on FDR:LA9, and R(E) from §6's DischargeResistor. Integrating the flux, rather than dividing by di/dt, is robust to the 12.5 µs sample noise. Report the secant λ/i and the incremental dλ/di against the resistor current and against time since commutation, per discharge, with the spread across discharges. The sweep starts from the prefire current the arcs already divert, not from zero. For stainless steel, expect a near-constant, mostly geometric inductance, with any eddy or shell contribution visible as a dependence on time rather than on current. State the measured value, its current and time dependence, and what the carbon-steel shell may add.
  • The magnetisation history as a measured fact. From the store, state each discharge's polarity and sequence, so the regime question is answered for the test resistor even though its material is different.

The material per section comes from the prototype test. 48NZDV v1.0 measured a TF module and a single section at Efremov on 11–12 April 2016. The S3 coordinator read these values from the report's plots by eye (private copy at data/sources/idm/48NZDV_v1_0.pdf); the external buses measured 2 µH, and "full" values include them.

ObjectRegimeWithout busesFull
TF module (4 sections in parallel)residual magnetisation≈0.4–0.6 µH, settling ≈0.45 µH, nearly flat 5–45 kA (Figs 4–5, pp. 8–9)≈2.4–2.6 µH
TF moduleremagnetisation, both polarities≈2.6 µH at 3–5 kA falling to ≈1.9 µH at 30 kA (Figs 9–10, 14)≈4.6 → 3.9 µH
Section aloneremagnetisation≈12 µH at 1–3 kA falling to ≈5.6 µH at 10 kA (Fig. 21, p. 19)≈14 → 7.6 µH
Section aloneresidual magnetisation≈1.4–1.5 µH, flat 2–8 kA (Figs 25–26, p. 21)≈3.4 µH

The report concludes that remagnetisation gives 4–5 times the residual-magnetisation value, and that measured values are about half of 7LDTQA's estimate. Build from these a per-section material model, one curve per regime against section current, with the 2 µH bus separated out. Then scale it to every ITER FDR by sections in parallel (current per section = I/Npar), modules in series and the bus inductance. S9BRS4 v2.0 gives the arrangement per coil (pp. 12–17, 35–38, from OCR of image-only pages, not visually checked):

FDRModules in seriesSections per moduleR at 20 °C
CS3U920.110 Ω

CS3L820.098 Ω
PF1530.0409 Ω

Every row gives 24.4–24.7 mΩ per section, which confirms that one common section underlies all of them. For the bus, take 7JQSNL v1.3 (PDF 11–13, Table 5) as the design stray: 3 µH for the resistor-to-breaker cable, with 4–5 mΩ. Set 48NZDV's measured 2 µH external bus beside it as the comparison. Neither is a measured per-coil bus geometry, and the record says so. A TF FDR's current is unipolar, so it sits in the residual regime. CS and PF currents reverse within a pulse, so successive fast discharges can come at either polarity; the remagnetisation regime is the conservative case there, and the record says which regime each coil's FDR is assigned and why. Give the result as tables in the energy-secant form §4's library accepts, so the report session can pass them to fast_discharge_unit in place of 7LDTQA's, and compare them point by point with 7LDTQA's CS1 and TF rows.

Done when the record docs/research/tf-cold-test-fdr-inductance.html gives:

  • the cold-test FDR's flux linkage, secant and incremental inductance against current and time for every current discharge, with the spread, the polarity history and the stated construction;
  • the per-section material model per regime, with the bus separated;
  • the scaled tables for TF, CS1 and one PF coil of each section count, in the library's form, beside 7LDTQA's;
  • a figure, rendered and inspected, showing the cold-test inductance against current and the per-section curves against 7LDTQA.

Checks:

  • Positive: a synthetic resistor trace built with a known inductance, passed through the same flux-linkage identification and sample rate, returns that inductance within 5 %.
  • Positive: the scaled TF module reproduces 48NZDV's module values from its section values within the 4.4/4 section-to-module ratio the report measured, or the record says why not.
  • Negative: replacing the measured vR by R(E)·i alone gives an identified inductance indistinguishable from zero.
  • Negative: raising R(E) by 2 % makes λ drift linearly in time, and the record shows the identification flags that drift rather than reading it as inductance.

§ Decisions

What filter was fitted to the MCTB supply before the TF17 test, and with which inductance, capacitance and damping resistance? No accessible IDM record holds it. If no values are known, §8 sizes an assumed filter to TF17's measured transfer and says so.

The lead reported on 20 October 2026 that no filter was added and that the mitigation was single-converter operation. The 80 kHz archive agrees. On TF17 the 300 Hz line dominates at about three times TF07's, which a 12-pulse pair would cancel. The 25 Hz loop line falls by about 100 times. The DC-line-to-converter ratio is unchanged at 300 and 600 Hz. §8 models TF17 as one unit with one PI loop.

Two corrections to §12 before it dispatches

The content review of 20 October 2026 (run r-20261020T200128211312) found two defects in §12. They are recorded here rather than edited in now, because §12 is not built in this wave and an edit would re-open the review gate for the nodes that are. Act on both before §12 dispatches:

  • Dependency. §12 declares a dependency on quench-detection-converter-pickup §3, but its stated reason, the second-order stage and detector-rate sampling, is now on main. Ask the QD session what §3 still supplies to §12, such as the per-line bridge transfer or the time-domain dwell path. Name it in the section, or drop the dependency so §12 runs once §10 closes.
  • Agreement check. The check that the line path's residual and the time-domain peak agree within the pair scatter compares unlike quantities: residual returns 2Σ|Af|, an envelope over line phases, while the time-domain path returns the largest filtered sample. Compare the line path with a coherent time-domain reconstruction from the same coefficients, or state the envelope as an upper bound on the peak, so a disagreement points at the front end and not at phase cancellation.

A current-dependent resistor inductance in the FDU owner

The S3 coordinator found that the IDM's FDR-plus-bus inductance is an energy secant, Ls = 2W/I², which falls with current (7LDTQA Tables 2.5–2.6, register row at commit 1451c36a). For CS1 with steel buses it is 94.9 µH at 6 kA, 29.0 µH at 28 kA and 20.6 µH at 45 kA. The TF row of 7LDTQA v1.0 Table 2.5 (p. 26), read through Lucy on 20 October 2026, is 143, 119, 96.4, 79.7, 57.2, 49.2, 34.4, 32.2 and 26.0 µH at 6, 8, 10, 14, 20, 28, 45, 49 and 70 kA; S9BRS4 v2.0 (p. 25) points to it. 7LDTQA forms the magnetic-material part as 2W/I² and adds the external inductance, including the busbars, which is linear. 778SPD Table 1.2.1-1 makes the CS FDR limit transient-inclusive (6.5 kV at main-breaker operation), so the full terminal voltage, R plus L, is what is judged. At the 6 kA constant, CS1U reads 6.82 kV with a 4 mF snubber, above the limit.

The inductance sees the resistor branch's own current, which sweeps from zero to the coil current in milliseconds during commutation. Because the table is an energy secant rather than a flux secant λ/I, the consistent incremental inductance is Ld(I) = W′(I)/I = Ls + (I/2)·dLs/dI, with W = ∫ i dλ and λ = ∫ Ld di. Interpolate W(I) = Ls·I²/2 monotonically between the nodes. Below the first point, hold the first value as a stated assumption. Above the last point, continue the last interval's Ld. For CS1 steel the interval values are about 51, 34, 36, 26, 20.5 and 15.3 µH. The flux-secant reading λ = Ls·I would give roughly half of these and understate the stray voltage. A linear interpolation of the secant gives negative values, which are unphysical.

The 6 kA constant bounds Ld from above. The full-current secant does not bound it from below: CS1's Ld at 28–45 kA is about 15 µH against the 20.6 µH secant at 45 kA. The owner change stays inside src/power_convertor/fast_discharge_unit.py as a companion source updated each step, because switched_circuit.py is held by another node. The default stays constant, so every held row is unchanged. No inductance for the cold-test FDR, constant or tabulated, is in the accessible IDM (D9XWQ5 v3.2, GJ4JX4 v1.2; some records are withheld), so the cold test cannot check the table.

Done when: Ld > 0 on [0, 1.5× the last point] for the CS1 and TF tables; W(I) reproduces Ls·I²/2 at every node; Ld lies below the secant wherever the secant falls; and a constant table reproduces the constant-L rows to a relative 1e-9. The last two checks were asked for by the report session (coil-supply-report-rebuild §5 depends on this section).

PF1 passive-response prior for §11's PF1 case, read through Lucy on 21 October 2026:

  • Coil and dump. Self-inductance 707.6 mH, with a starting dump resistance of 60.3 mΩ for a 48 kA discharge (9ALK99 v1.1 pp. 4–5). The initial L/R is about 11.7 s, and FQ9RWN v1.0 models τ = 11.5 s. The MCTB overview 8RKR98 v1.0 gives 700 mH, 48 kA and 0.806 GJ.
  • No separate passive structure. FQ9RWN v1.0 p. 4 states the PF1 case has none: the thick jacket is electrically connected to the cable. No k², winding-to-casing mutual inductance or casing time constant is documented.
  • Coupling loss only. The passive response is the conductor coupling loss, nτ = 0.2042 − 0.0156B + 0.000153257·B·I s (B in T, I in kA, n = 2; 9ALK99 v1.1 p. 10). That is 350 kJ of AC loss in the winding pack for the 48 kA discharge (p. 11), about 0.04 % of the stored energy.

So the PF1 plant carries this small conductor coupling loss as its stated prior, not a casing mode like TF's §5 mode. 7L8PNZ v1.1's vacuum-vessel walls are a tokamak case, not the test bench.

Correction to c-s11-pf1-prior. The 60.3 mΩ there is the dump resistor's starting resistance during a fast discharge (9ALK99), not PF1's own loop resistance. PF1 is superconducting. In flat top and during ramps its loop resistance is only the warm busbars, leads and converter path, of the order of the cold test's measured DC path (about 0.23–0.24 mΩ on TF17 and TF07). Holding 48 kA therefore needs about 11 V plus the converter's own drops, and the 40 A/s discharge needs L·dI/dt ≈ 0.708 H × 40 A/s ≈ 28 V. Both lie within a TF-class unit's 36–54 V. The first §11 delivery read the 60.3 mΩ as the coil's resistance and concluded that PF1 needs 2.9 kV and a different converter; that conclusion is wrong and is being repaired.
